Manhattan distance is distinct from similarity scores, such as cosine similarity, where larger values indicate greater similarity, whereas Manhattan distance is a distance metric.
In the context of clustering, when the objective is to minimize the sum of distances, the appropriate centroid for a cluster using Manhattan distance is the median of the points in that cluster.
An example calculation for two points A and B is d_Manhattan(A, B) = |1 − 4| + |1 − 5| = 3 + 4 = 7, illustrating the summation of absolute coordinate differences.
Cosine similarity is a similarity score where a larger value indicates greater similarity.
Cosine similarity measures the cosine of the angle between two vectors.
When the cosine similarity is 1, the angle between the vectors is 0 degrees, meaning they point in the same direction and are identical except for length.
When the cosine similarity is 0, the angle is 90 degrees, indicating the vectors are perpendicular and do not share any terms.
When the cosine similarity is -1, the vectors point in exactly opposite directions.
The calculation involves normalizing the vectors by dividing them by their lengths, which results in vectors of length 1.
Cosine similarity does not take the length of the data objects into account due to normalization.
For unit-length vectors, the cosine measure is calculated by taking a simple inner product.
Cosine similarity is useful for sparse data, such as documents represented as vectors where components record word frequencies.
Cosine similarity can reduce computation time when many similarities are calculated.
In the context of clustering, cosine similarity is used as a proximity measure in K-means style algorithms.
Cosine similarity is included in the class of Bregman divergences, which can serve as the basis for clustering algorithms with convergence properties similar to standard K-means.
The Rand Index is an external validation measure used to evaluate clustering by comparing the cluster structure against true class labels.
The Rand Index is calculated using the formula: Rand Index = (f11 + f00) / (f11 + f10 + f01 + f00).
The Rand Index includes pairs of objects that are correctly separated in both the class structure and the clustering (f00) in its calculation.
The Rand Index is a similarity-oriented measure that operates by comparing pairs of objects.
The Rand Index is often higher than the Jaccard Coefficient because it includes f00 pairs in its calculation.
The calculation counts only pairs of distinct objects; self-pairs are not included in the Rand Index computation.
The Rand Index does not require the original feature values once the cluster assignments and class labels are available.
The Rand Index is computed through class similarity and cluster similarity matrices.
An adjusted version of the Rand Index exists and is based on the multivariate hypergeometric distribution, which can be used to compute a p-value.
The Jaccard coefficient is a similarity measure used to evaluate the similarity between two binary vectors.
The Jaccard coefficient is defined by the formula Jaccard Coefficient = f11 / (f11 + f10 + f01).
The Jaccard coefficient ignores f00, focusing only on pairs that are together in at least one of the two structures.
The Jaccard coefficient is frequently employed as a cluster validity measure.
The Jaccard coefficient is often symbolized by j.
The Jaccard coefficient is particularly useful in contexts involving asymmetric binary attributes such as transaction data.
For example, given f00=4, f01=2, f10=2, and f11=2, the Jaccard coefficient is calculated as 2 / (2 + 2 + 2) = 0.33.
The measure can be extended to more than two variables using multidimensional contingency tables.
An extended version, known as the Extended Jaccard Coefficient or Tanimoto Coefficient, is used for document data and reduces to the standard Jaccard coefficient for binary attributes.
The Jaccard coefficient distinguishes itself from other measures like the Rand statistic (or Simple Matching Coefficient), which includes f00 in its calculation.
A similarity matrix is a square matrix that stores the pairwise similarity between every pair of objects in a data set.
The similarity between two objects is a numerical measure of the degree to which they are alike; higher values indicate greater similarity.
Similarities are usually nonnegative and are often scaled to the interval [0, 1], where 0 represents no similarity and 1 represents complete similarity.
This scaling is frequently achieved through linear transformations that map the original range of similarity or dissimilarity values to [0, 1], preserving the relative distances between points.
In the context of clustering, the similarity matrix is used to evaluate the 'goodness' of a clustering by comparing it against an ideal cluster similarity matrix.
The ideal matrix is constructed by assigning a value of 1 to an entry if the corresponding pair of points belongs to the same cluster, and 0 otherwise.

When the rows and columns of the matrix are sorted so that objects belonging to the same cluster are grouped together, the ideal cluster similarity matrix exhibits a block diagonal structure, with non-zero values inside the blocks representing intra-cluster similarity and zero values elsewhere.
The correlation between the actual similarity matrix and this ideal matrix serves as a measure of cluster validity, a metric known in the clustering validation literature as Hubert's Γ statistic.
The similarity matrix can also be used for visual inspection of clustering results.
By ordering the matrix with respect to cluster labels and plotting it, the patterns displayed can reveal the relationships and separation between clusters.
Well-separated clusters are illustrated by a reordered similarity matrix where high similarity values are concentrated within cluster blocks.

In supervised or semi-supervised contexts, the cluster similarity matrix can be compared against a class similarity matrix—defined as 1 if two objects belong to the same class and 0 otherwise—to derive validity measures such as the Rand Index or Jaccard Coefficient.
In these pair-by-pair comparisons, diagonal entries (comparing an object to itself) are typically excluded, as only pairs of distinct objects are counted.
A missing value is a data quality issue where an attribute value or an entire data object is absent from a dataset.
Missing values can occur because information was not collected or because certain attributes are not applicable to all objects.
Missing values are distinct from other data quality issues such as spurious or duplicate objects, and inconsistencies where data is present but logically incorrect.
Handling missing values is a critical step in data analysis because even partially specified data objects contain information, and ignoring them can make reliable analysis difficult or impossible.
The approach to handling missing values depends on the specific machine learning algorithm being used.
Naïve Bayes classifiers handle missing values by ignoring them during training and using only non-missing values for testing.
Bayesian networks handle missing values by treating them as unobserved nodes and marginalizing out their effect.
Logistic regression and artificial neural networks (ANN) cannot handle missing values and typically require instances with missing values to be discarded.

Decision tree classifiers offer several specific methods for handling missing values in test instances, including the probabilistic split method, the surrogate split method, and the separate class method.
General strategies for dealing with missing values include deletion and imputation.
Deletion involves eliminating objects or attributes with missing values, which is expedient if only a few objects are affected but risky if many are missing or if the attributes are critical.
Imputation involves estimating missing values, such as by interpolating in time series, using nearest neighbors, or using the mean (for continuous attributes) or mode (for categorical attributes).
There is no universal imputation method that performs best for all classifiers.
The missingness mechanism describes how the probability of a value being missing depends on observed and unobserved data.
Under missing at random (MAR), missingness may depend on observed values but not directly on the missing values.
Missing completely at random (MCAR) is a special case of MAR where missingness depends on neither observed nor unobserved data.
If MAR does not hold and missingness depends on both observed values and the missing value itself, the mechanism is called not missing at random (NMAR) or missing not at random (MNAR).
The probability of missingness under MAR can be expressed as P(B|X_obs,X_mis,ζ) = P(B|X_obs,ζ).
The probability of missingness under MCAR can be expressed as P(B|X_obs,X_mis,ζ) = P(B|ζ).
The deletion strategy handles missing values by removing data objects or attributes that contain missing entries.
Eliminating objects can be expedient when only a small number of objects are affected.
Eliminating attributes must be used cautiously because an attribute with missing values may still be important to the analysis.
Deletion gives unbiased estimates under the MCAR assumption.
Deletion reduces statistical power even when the data are MCAR.
When the data are not MCAR, deletion can introduce bias.
Imputation is the process of replacing missing values in a dataset with estimated values.
Imputation is distinguished from deletion strategies, which remove cases containing missing data.
Imputation methods generally fall into two broad categories: statistical methods and machine learning methods.
Statistical methods model the underlying probability distribution of the data.
Machine learning methods do not require assuming a specific underlying distribution but still rely on the Missing At Random (MAR) assumption.
Maximum Likelihood Imputation and Expectation-Maximization (EM) are examples of statistical methods.
K-means Clustering Imputation (KMI) and Fuzzy K-means Imputation are examples of machine learning methods.
KMI works by clustering data into K groups, where each cluster is represented by a centroid.
Fuzzy K-means imputation extends KMI by allowing objects to belong to multiple clusters with different membership degrees.
Evaluating imputation methods is challenging, and metrics like Mean Squared Error (MSE) or Root Mean Squared Error (RMSE) are commonly used.
In supervised settings, metrics like Wilson’s Noise Ratio may be used to assess the impact of imputation on the learning task.
Informative missingness corresponds to the source's not-missing-at-random (NMAR/MNAR) case.
The probability that a value is missing depends on the missing value itself as well as on observed information.
The missingness mechanism cannot be reduced to a function of only the observed values as in MAR.
The missingness process itself carries information about the unobserved value.
Obtaining an unbiased estimate requires modeling the missingness process as well.
Data integration is the process of merging data elements from different sources into a single data set.
The integration process requires building a data map to establish how each instance should be arranged in a common structure.
Different attribute names or table schemes from various sources produce uneven examples that need to be consolidated.
Attribute values may represent the same concept with different names, creating inconsistencies in the instances obtained.
When data is obtained from relational databases, it is usually flattened and gathered together into one single record.
Some database frameworks enable the user to provide a map to directly traverse the database through in-database access utilities.
Using in-database mining tools has the advantage of not having to extract and create an external file for the data.
Extracting the data to an external file can be faster for processing and modeling if the data is already preprocessed and completely fits in memory.
If the integration process is not properly performed, redundancies and inconsistencies will appear, resulting in a decrease of the accuracy and speed of subsequent data mining processes.
Matching the schema from different sources presents a notorious problem that usually does not come alone, including inconsistent and duplicated tuples as well as redundant and correlated attributes.
Automatic approaches used to integrate the data can be found in the literature, from techniques that match and find the schemas of the data to automatic procedures that reconcile different schemas.
Even after correct integration, the data may still contain errors, including missing data, wrong data, and non-standard representation of the same data.
Dirty data can have varying degrees of impact depending on the data mining algorithm, but it is difficult to quantify such an impact.
A high proportion of dirty data can result in an unreliable model when applying a data mining process.
An attribute is redundant when it can be derived from another attribute or set of them, or when it is strongly correlated with another attribute in the data.
Redundancy in attributes is a problem that should be avoided because it can cause an increase in data set size and modeling time, and may induce overfitting in the obtained model.
Inconsistencies in dimension or attribute names can cause redundancies.
When examples come from different sources and have to be merged in a single data set, detecting and eliminating redundant attributes is necessary.
Redundancies in attributes can be detected using correlation analysis.
For nominal attributes, the chi-squared test is commonly applied to detect redundancy.
For numeric attributes, the correlation coefficient and covariance are typically used to detect redundancy.
A contingency table is created to compute the chi-squared value for nominal attributes.
The chi-squared test checks the hypothesis that two attributes are independent.
The correlation coefficient for two numerical attributes is computed as the sum over i from 1 to m of (ai - A_bar)(bi - B_bar) / (m σA σB).
Different classifiers handle redundant attributes in different ways.
Decision trees can handle redundant attributes by selecting only one of them for splitting.
Logistic regression can handle redundant attributes that are duplicates of each other without degrading classification performance.
Linear SVM can handle redundant attributes by learning similar weights for the duplicate attributes.
Rule-based classifiers can easily handle redundant attributes that are highly correlated with one another.
Bayesian networks can handle correlated or redundant attributes by expressing richer forms of conditional independence.
Artificial neural networks can handle redundant attributes by receiving similar weights for them without degrading the quality of the classifier.
A large number of redundant attributes can bias proximity measures and affect the performance of nearest neighbor classifiers.
Duplicate tuples are repeated instances of data records that appear in a dataset.
Duplicate tuples can arise from the use of denormalized tables or errors in the data entry process.
Duplicates waste storage space and computing time for data mining algorithms and can serve as a source of inconsistency.
Entry errors can cause slight differences in attribute values, resulting in instances that are substantively identical but are treated as distinct.
Duplicate tuples can emerge during the data integration process, where matching schemas from different sources can introduce redundancies and inconsistencies.
The detection of tuple duplication is a specific preprocessing step in data mining.
There is no formal algorithm or procedure provided for resolving duplicate tuples in the source material.
Inconsistent values are data quality issues where recorded attribute values differ from the true values or violate established constraints.
Inconsistent values can occur when information is sourced from different systems with varying measurement standards, leading to instances that are actually the same but not identified as such.
A specific form of inconsistency arises when attribute values fall outside the established range, a condition usually indicated in the associated metadata for the data set.
An example of inconsistent values is an address field where the specified zip code area is not contained within the listed city, which may result from transposed digits or misread handwritten forms.
Inconsistent values must be resolved when two objects represent a single entity but have differing attribute values.
Detecting and, if possible, correcting inconsistent values is important to ensure data integrity.
Data cleaning is the first step in data preprocessing, specifically defined as the detection and correction of data inaccuracies.
The primary goal of data cleaning is to filter or repair dirty data to ensure that the knowledge extracted by DM algorithms is accurate and that the algorithms can effectively handle the data.
Dirty data typically manifests in two main forms: missing data and wrong (noisy) data.
The sources of dirty data errors include data entry errors, data update errors, data transmission errors, and bugs in the data processing system.
Data cleaning is distinct from data normalization and transformation, which are used to adapt the data set to the specific needs of the DM algorithm rather than correcting inaccuracies.
The impact of dirty data varies by algorithm; for example, decision trees, artificial neural networks (ANNs), and distance-based algorithms like KNN are known to be susceptible to noise.
Data cleaning is a foundational technique required to improve the accuracy and efficiency of subsequent data mining processes.
Without data cleaning, the presence of dirty data can lead to less reliable models or prevent algorithms from functioning properly.
Normalization and transformation are data preprocessing techniques used to adapt a data set to the needs of a subsequent data mining algorithm.
A variable transformation is a transformation applied to all the values of a variable, meaning that for each object, the transformation is applied to the value of the variable for that object.
If only the magnitude of a variable is important, the values can be transformed by taking the absolute value.
Normalization usually refers to a particular case of min-max normalization in which the final interval is [0, 1], meaning the new minimum is 0 and the new maximum is 1.
The interval [-1, 1] is also typical when normalizing data.
The formula for min-max normalization is: v' = new-min_A + R * ((v - min_A) / (max_A - min_A)), where max_A and min_A are the original maximum and minimum attribute values respectively.
Normalization is very common in data sets being prepared for learning methods based on distances.
Rescaling all data to the same range of values avoids attributes with a large max_A - min_A difference dominating over others in distance calculations.
Normalization helps weights to converge faster in artificial neural networks (ANNs).
Transformation or normalization of the data is needed to obtain a proper similarity measure, such as when time series have trends or periodic patterns that significantly impact similarity.

A specific transformation useful for obtaining a new variable that is very likely to behave like a normally distributed one involves using the rank of the observation and the cumulative normal function.
This transformation cannot be applied separately to the training and test partitions; it is only recommended when the test and training data is the same.
A confusion matrix is a table that summarizes the performance of a classifier by comparing predicted labels against the true labels of instances in a test set.
For a binary classification problem, the matrix is organized with rows representing the true class and columns representing the predicted class.
The confusion matrix contains four specific counts: True Positives (TP), False Negatives (FN), False Positives (FP), and True Negatives (TN).
True Positives (TP) are actual positives predicted as positive.
False Negatives (FN) are actual positives predicted as negative.
False Positives (FP) are actual negatives predicted as positive.
True Negatives (TN) are actual negatives predicted as negative.
The confusion matrix is used to evaluate models trained on independent training and test sets to ensure accurate prediction of unseen instances.
The counts in the confusion matrix are often summarized into single-value evaluation measures, such as accuracy, to facilitate the comparison of relative performance between different models.
The confusion matrix is also applicable in contexts such as clustering, where it provides the most detailed information for evaluating the performance of a specific cluster against a class.
Accuracy is a metric used to evaluate the quality of classification rules and classifiers.
Accuracy is defined as the fraction of instances triggered by the rule whose class labels are equal to the predicted class.
For binary classification, accuracy is calculated as the sum of true positives and true negatives divided by the total number of predictions.
Accuracy can also be expressed generally as the number of correct predictions divided by the number of all predictions.
Accuracy is an estimate based on a finite test set and is not guaranteed to be the exact true accuracy of the classifier.
A higher raw accuracy alone is not always a significant win; a raw accuracy difference is not automatically a significant win.
Accuracy can be misleading because it can hide poor positive-class performance, especially under class imbalance.
Larger test sets reduce sampling uncertainty associated with the measured accuracy.
Precision is an evaluation measure for binary classification that quantifies the fraction of correct predictions of the positive class over the total number of positive predictions.
The standard formula for precision is p = TP / (TP + FP), where TP represents true positives and FP represents false positives.
Precision is also referred to as the positive predicted value (PPV).

A classifier with high precision is likely to have most of its positive predictions correct, making it a useful measure for highly skewed test sets where positive predictions, even though small in numbers, are required to be mostly correct.

Precision is sensitive to class skew; when selecting a score threshold for a classifier, if the evaluation measure is precision, the skew of the validation set used for selection must be similar to that of the test set to ensure optimal performance.
In the context of statistical testing, precision is closely related to the false discovery rate (FDR), with the relationship precision = 1 - FDR.

Precision captures the effect of false positives but not false negatives; a classifier that is very conservative in classifying instances as positive to reduce false positives may end up having high precision but very poor recall.
A perfect classifier is characterized by precision = 1 and recall = 1.
Recall is a classifier evaluation metric that measures the proportion of actual positive instances correctly identified by the model.
Recall is defined by the formula Recall = TP / (TP + FN), where TP represents true positives and FN represents false negatives.
Recall is also known as sensitivity in the medical community.
A classifier with a high recall value has a high chance of correctly identifying the positive instances in the data.
In the information retrieval literature, this metric is also referred to as recall (r).
Recall is distinct from precision, which is based on predicted positives, and specificity, which is based on actual negatives.
An example calculation of recall is 2 / (2 + 1) = 2/3 = 0.667, or 66.7%.
Specificity is a classifier evaluation metric defined as the fraction of negative test instances correctly predicted by the classifier.
Specificity is calculated as the number of true negatives (TN) divided by the sum of true negatives and false positives (FP).
Specificity is also known as the true negative rate (TNR).
Specificity checks how many actual negatives were correctly rejected by the model.
Specificity is distinct from precision for the negative class because specificity uses actual negatives in the denominator, whereas negative predictive value uses predicted negatives.
A classifier with 5 true negatives and 2 false positives yields a specificity of 5/7, or approximately 71.4%.
Specificity is used alongside other metrics such as accuracy, precision, recall, and F-measure to provide a comprehensive view of classifier performance.
Specificity is particularly useful when the correct rejection of negative cases is a priority.
The F-measure combines precision p and recall r.
The source defines F_β = ((β² + 1)rp)/(r + β²p), where β controls the relative importance of recall and precision.
For β = 1, F1 = 2pr/(p + r), the harmonic mean of precision and recall.
Higher values indicate a better balance of the two measures.
A clean classification evaluation workflow separates model construction and model selection from final model evaluation.
Labeled data are partitioned so that training/model-selection data are kept separate from the test set;
The final selected model is then evaluated on a labeled test set that was not used to select it.
Test performance is obtained by comparing predicted labels with the true labels, for example through a confusion matrix and derived evaluation measures.
When a classifier is evaluated on N independent test instances, let X be the number classified correctly and let p be the model's true accuracy.
Under the binomial model, acc = X/N has mean p and variance p(1-p)/N.
For sufficiently large N, the binomial can be approximated by a normal distribution.
The confidence interval for p is given by [2N·acc + z² ± z√(z² + 4N·acc - 4N·acc²)] / [2(N + z²)], where z = Z_{α/2} for confidence level 1-α.
The interval becomes tighter as N increases.
To compare two models evaluated on independent test sets, their observed error rates and the number of instances in each set are needed.
The estimated variance of the difference in error rates is calculated using the formula σ̂_d² = e1(1-e1)/n1 + e2(1-e2)/n2.
The confidence interval for the true difference in error rates is given by d_t = d ± z_{α/2}σ̂_d at confidence level 1-α.
For sufficiently large test sets, the estimated variance formula can be applied.
If a two-sided confidence interval contains zero, the observed difference in error rates is not statistically significant at that confidence level.
The difference in error rates is denoted as d = e1 - e2, where e1 and e2 are the observed error rates on the two independent test sets.
The significance level, denoted by the Greek letter alpha (α), is a fixed constant in hypothesis testing whose value is decided before any tests are performed.
The significance level is defined as the probability of incurring a type I error, which is equal to the probability of the critical region under the null hypothesis.
A result is called statistically significant if it has a p-value lower than the pre-specified threshold α.
Common choices for the level of significance are 0.05 (5%) and 0.01 (1%).
In specific applications, such as a one-sided test, the significance level determines the critical value used for decision-making.
For example, at a significance level of 0.05, the critical value for a one-sided test is Z = 1.64.
The significance level serves as the target for controlling the Family-Wise Error Rate (FWER) in multiple testing scenarios.
Procedures like Bonferroni adjust the per-test significance level to ensure the overall FWER remains below α.
One-sided and two-sided tests are statistical procedures used to determine whether an observed result is a significant departure from the null hypothesis.
One-sided tests are categorized as right-tailed or left-tailed, while two-sided tests evaluate whether the result is extreme in either direction.
The distinction between one-sided and two-sided tests is reflected in the distribution of the significance level (alpha) across the tails of the null distribution.
A two-sided test with an alpha of 0.05 allocates 0.025 probability to each tail, whereas a one-sided test allocates the entire 0.05 probability to a single tail.
A low p-value indicates smaller probabilities in the tails of the null distribution, providing sufficient evidence to reject the null hypothesis.
A one-sided test asking whether model A is better than model B is distinct from a two-tailed test, which asks whether the classifiers are different in either direction.
A threshold of |Z| > 1.96 at alpha = 0.05 is normally used for a two-tailed test.
Test-set size controls sampling uncertainty in measured classifier performance.
Increasing the test sample size reduces sampling variance and tightens the confidence interval for the true accuracy.
The variance of the estimated accuracy is given by Var(acc) = p(1-p)/N, where p is the true accuracy and N is the test sample size.
Larger independent test samples support more precise performance estimates and significance assessments.
In comparisons of two models on independent test sets, the uncertainty in the observed error-rate difference contains terms proportional to 1/n1 and 1/n2, where n1 and n2 are the test sample sizes.
An ensemble classifier is a method that constructs a set of base classifiers from training data and performs classification by taking a vote on the predictions made by each base classifier.
The ensemble classifier predicts the class label of a test example by taking a majority vote on the predictions made by the base classifiers.
The base classifiers are often individually imperfect, but their combined decision can be more robust.
For classification, a common combination rule is majority voting, where the final prediction is determined by the majority of the individual predictions.
An alternate approach is to take a weighted majority vote, where the weight of a base classifier denotes its accuracy or relevance.
If the base classifiers are identical, then all the base classifiers will commit the same mistakes, and the error rate of the ensemble remains the same as the individual classifiers.
If the base classifiers are independent, then the ensemble makes a wrong prediction only if more than half of the base classifiers predict incorrectly.
The error rate of the ensemble classifier is lower than that of the individual classifiers when the base classifiers are independent.
The ensemble classifier performs worse than the base classifiers when the base classifier error rate is larger than 0.5.

Two necessary conditions for an ensemble classifier to perform better than a single classifier are: the base classifiers should be independent of each other, and the base classifiers should do better than a classifier that performs random guessing.

In practice, it is difficult to ensure total independence among the base classifiers, but improvements in classification accuracies have been observed in ensemble methods in which the base classifiers are somewhat correlated.

The ensemble of classifiers can be constructed in many ways, including by manipulating the training set, where multiple training sets are created by resampling the original data according to some sampling distribution and constructing a classifier from each training set.
Bagging and boosting are two examples of ensemble methods that manipulate their training sets.
The base classifiers for most of these approaches can be generated sequentially or in parallel.
Once an ensemble of classifiers has been learned, a test example is classified by combining the predictions made by the base classifiers.
The final prediction of the ensemble classifier is obtained by taking a weighted average of the predictions made by each base classifier.

The ensemble classifier can enhance the representation of the target function; even though each base classifier is a decision stump, combining the classifiers can lead to a decision boundary that mimics a decision tree of depth 2.

The ensemble classifier is a general method that can be applied to any classifier, and it is used to improve the performance of a single classifier by combining the predictions of multiple base classifiers.
Majority voting is a combination rule used in ensemble classification to derive a single final prediction from the outputs of multiple base classifiers.
The final prediction is the class that receives the most votes.
This method is particularly common in random forests, where the final prediction is obtained by majority voting over the individual decision trees.

The ensemble is strongest when the individual trees are reasonably accurate and their errors are not perfectly correlated, as this diversity helps reduce the high variance associated with single decision trees.
A weighted majority vote is an alternative approach where the weight of a base classifier denotes its accuracy or relevance, but in standard majority voting, every vote has equal impact.
In the context of k-nearest neighbors, majority voting assigns the test instance to the majority class of its nearest neighbors, with ties potentially resolved by random choice.
The procedure involves sending a test instance through all base classifiers or trees and combining their predictions using this voting mechanism.
A random forest is an ensemble of decision trees, where each tree is trained using randomness so that the trees are not all identical.
The method manipulates both the training instances and the input features to create diversity among the base classifiers.
The training data is represented as a set of instances D = {(x1, y1), (x2, y2), ..., (xN, yN)}.
The induction process for each tree involves drawing a bootstrap sample from the original training set by sampling N instances with replacement.
A decision tree is then trained on the bootstrap sample, often grown deeply and without heavy pruning, meaning the trees are unpruned and allowed to grow until every leaf is pure.
At every split, the tree considers only a random subset of features and chooses the best split from that subset.
The number of attributes to be selected at every node, p, is a hyper-parameter of the random forest classifier.
For classification, the final prediction is made by combining the trees using majority voting: ŷ = majority{h1(x), h2(x), ..., hB(x)}.
The two main random components are bootstrap sampling of instances and random feature selection at each split.
This approach reduces the variance of the trees without negatively impacting their low bias, making random forests robust to overfitting and computationally fast even in high-dimensional settings.
Boosting is an iterative ensemble procedure that adaptively changes the distribution of training examples so that base classifiers increasingly focus on examples that are hard to classify.
Boosting assigns a weight to each training example and may adaptively change the weight at the end of each boosting round.
The algorithm begins by assigning equal weights to all examples, then draws a sample according to the sampling distribution to obtain a new training set.
A classifier is built from this training set and used to classify all examples in the original data.

At the end of each boosting round, the weights of the training examples are updated: examples that are classified incorrectly have their weights increased, while those classified correctly have their weights decreased.
As the boosting rounds proceed, examples that are the hardest to classify tend to become even more prevalent in the sampling distribution.
The final ensemble is obtained by aggregating the base classifiers obtained from each boosting round.
In the AdaBoost implementation, the prediction made by each classifier is weighted rather than using a majority voting scheme, which allows the algorithm to penalize models that have poor accuracy.
If any intermediate round produces an error rate higher than 50%, the weights are reverted back to their original uniform values and the resampling procedure is repeated.

The training error of the ensemble decreases exponentially, leading to fast convergence, although the technique can be susceptible to overfitting due to its tendency to focus on wrongly classified examples.
The class imbalance problem occurs when the training set has an unbalanced representation of classes, typically with a minority class that is not well-represented.

Class imbalance poses two challenges for classification: many classification methods work well only with balanced class representation, and a classifier trained over an imbalanced data set is biased toward the majority class.
In binary classification, the minority class is referred to as the positive class, while the majority class is referred to as the negative class.
The class imbalance problem is particularly relevant in model evaluation, where detection rate and false alarm rate are metrics that are not sensitive to skewness in the class distribution.

In the presence of class imbalance, the behavior of an algorithm over small false positive rate values is often more meaningful for comparison than the performance over all false positive rate values.
Assessing the true positive rate achieved by a classifier in the first few instances with highest scores, without incurring a large false positive rate, is important in many applications.
The precision-recall (PR) curve is an alternate approach for measuring the aggregate performance of a classifier, which is especially useful in the presence of class imbalance.

The PR curve helps to magnify the differences between classifiers in the left portion of the PR curve, providing a deeper insight into the performance of classifiers than the ROC curves, especially in the early retrieval range of operating points.
Oversampling is a technique used to create a balanced training set by artificially generating new positive examples to address class imbalance.

A simple approach to oversampling involves duplicating every positive instance a specific number of times, where the duplication factor is determined by the ratio of the number of negative training instances to the number of positive training instances.

The duplication method is analogous to doubling the weight of positive instances during the training stage, an effect that can alternatively be achieved by assigning higher weights to positive instances than negative instances.
Assigning higher weights to positive instances than negative instances is a method compatible with classifiers such as logistic regression, artificial neural networks, and support vector machines.
The Synthetic Minority Oversampling Technique (SMOTE) generates synthetic positive instances in the neighborhood of existing positive instances.

The SMOTE procedure first determines the k-nearest positive neighbors of every positive instance, then generates a synthetic positive instance at some intermediate point along the line segment joining the instance to one of its randomly chosen k-nearest neighbors.
The SMOTE process is repeated until the desired number of positive instances is reached.

A limitation of the duplication method is that replicated positive examples have an artificially lower variance compared to their true distribution, which can bias the classifier to the specific distribution of training instances and lead to poor generalizability.

A limitation of SMOTE is that it can only generate new positive instances within the convex hull of the existing positive class, meaning it does not improve the representation of the positive class outside the boundary of existing positive instances.
Undersampling and oversampling provide useful directions for generating balanced training sets in the presence of class imbalance.

Undersampling is a sampling method used to create balanced training sets in the presence of class imbalance by reducing the frequency of the majority class to match the frequency of the minority class.

Undersampling is one of two primary strategies for ensuring that a learning algorithm is trained over a data set with adequate representation of both the majority and minority classes, the other being oversampling.

To illustrate the procedure, consider a training set containing 100 positive examples and 1000 negative examples, where a random sample of 100 examples is selected from the negative class and used with the 100 positive examples to create a balanced training set.

One limitation of undersampling is that some useful negative examples, particularly those closer to the actual decision boundary, may not be chosen for training, which can result in an inferior classification model.
Another limitation of undersampling is that the smaller sample of negative instances may have a higher variance than the larger original set.
Undersampling and oversampling provide complementary directions for generating balanced training sets, each with distinct strengths and weaknesses.
A cost matrix assigns a cost or benefit to each possible classification outcome, such as false negative, false positive, true positive, and true negative.
The expected cost of a model is the probability-weighted sum of these outcome costs: C(M) = P(FN)c_FN + P(FP)c_FP + P(TP)c_TP + P(TN)c_TN.
When costs are the decision criterion, models or operating points are compared by their expected cost and lower expected cost is preferred.
Cost-Sensitive Classification is an approach to model evaluation and learning that accounts for the differing consequences of misclassification errors.
The method involves evaluating decision quality using a cost matrix, where the choice of a model is determined by minimizing the expected cost.
Cost-Sensitive Classification is motivated by the need for evaluation metrics that are sensitive to class skew and capture performance criteria beyond simple accuracy.
The foundations of this area include the study of cost matrix properties and various methods for incorporating cost information into learning algorithms.
Algorithm-independent methods include AdaCost, MetaCost, and costing.
Cost-sensitive boosting is also a recognized technique in this domain.
In a specific evaluation context, a model was selected based on having the lowest expected cost of 0.390.
RIPPER is a rule induction algorithm that generates classification rules directly from data.
RIPPER uses a validation set to prevent model overfitting.
RIPPER employs a sequential covering scheme to induce rules.
RIPPER eliminates all positive and negative examples covered by a generated rule.
RIPPER stops adding rules if a new rule increases the total description length of the rule set by at least d bits.
The default value of d is 64 bits.
RIPPER stops adding rules if the error rate of the rule on the validation set exceeds 50%.
RIPPER prunes rules to improve generalization errors based on their performance on the validation set.
Pruning is done starting from the last conjunct added to the rule, removing a conjunct if a specific metric improves after pruning.
The pruning metric is monotonically related to the rule's accuracy on the validation set and involves the number of positive and negative examples in the validation set covered by the rule.
The original rule covers only positive examples, but the pruned rule may cover some negative examples in the training set.
A receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve plots the true positive rate (TPR) on the y-axis against the false positive rate (FPR) on the x-axis as the classifier's score threshold is varied.
The curve begins at (0,0) when every instance is predicted negative and ends at (1,1) when every instance is predicted positive;
a perfect classifier reaches (FPR=0, TPR=1).
Each point is an operating point corresponding to a particular threshold.
Random guessing lies on the main diagonal: if an instance is predicted positive with fixed probability p irrespective of its attributes, then TPR = FPR = p, so the operating point is (p,p).
ROC space uses FPR on the x-axis and TPR on the y-axis.
The point (0,1) represents a perfect classifier with no false positives and all positives detected.
The point (0,0) represents predicting every instance as negative.
The point (1,1) represents predicting every instance as positive.
Good operating points lie toward the upper-left corner.
Random guessing lies on the diagonal from (0,0) to (1,1).
The Area Under the ROC Curve (AUC) is a measure used to summarize the aggregate behavior of a classifier across all operating points.
A perfect classifier yields an AUC of 1, while an algorithm that performs random guessing results in an AUC of 0.5.
The AUC is also described as the number of correctly ranked positive-negative pairs.
The AUC is insensitive to class skew in the test set.
The AUC serves as a performance metric for machine learning algorithms, providing a single value that reflects overall classification quality.

A higher AUC for one algorithm does not guarantee that it is strictly better than another, as this would require the ROC curve of the first algorithm to dominate the second across all operating points.
If the ROC curves of two classifiers intersect, it is difficult to assess their relative quality using the AUC alone.

The AUC has been considered an incoherent measure of performance because it may use different scales when comparing different classifiers, although coherent interpretations have been proposed in the literature.
The AUC distinguishes itself from the Area Under the Precision-Recall Curve (AUC-PR), which varies with changing skew.
A classification threshold or cutoff converts a classifier score s(x) into a class decision: an instance is predicted positive when its score exceeds the selected threshold.
Changing the threshold produces different operating points.
The source selects an optimal threshold on validation data by sorting the observed scores, treating each unique score as a candidate threshold and computing a chosen evaluation measure E(s).
The selected optimal threshold s* is the one that maximizes the chosen evaluation measure E(s), denoted as s* = argmax_s E(s).
The selected s* is then treated as a learned hyper-parameter for classifying future instances.
Changing the classification threshold changes the set of instances predicted positive and therefore changes the confusion-matrix counts from which precision and recall are computed.
Raising or lowering the threshold can trade precision against recall.
F1 combines precision and recall as F1 = 2·precision·recall/(precision + recall).
If a threshold is selected to optimize precision, recall, or F1, class skew matters for skew-sensitive measures such as precision and F1.
Cost-based model selection compares ROC operating points using the expected cost implied by the class prior and a cost matrix.
The preferred model or operating point is the one with the lowest expected cost under the specified costs and class prior.
The expected cost C(M) can be calculated using the formula C(M) = P(FN)c_FN + P(FP)c_FP + P(TP)c_TP + P(TN)c_TN.
The outcome probabilities P(FN), P(FP), P(TP), and P(TN) are determined by the true positive rate (TPR), false positive rate (FPR), and the positive-class prior p.
The true positive rate (TPR) and false positive rate (FPR) determine the outcome probabilities, allowing the expected cost of each ROC point or model to be computed.
The holdout method is a model evaluation technique in which the available dataset is split once into two parts: a training set and a test set.
The model is learned over the training set, and the resulting test error rate corresponds exactly to the performance of that specific model learned over that specific training set.

This distinguishes the holdout method from k-fold cross-validation, where a different model is learned at every run and the performance of every one of the k models on their respective test folds is aggregated to compute the overall test error rate.

In cross-validation, the computed error reflects the expected generalization error rate of the model selection approach when applied on a training set of the same size as one of the training folds, rather than the performance of a single model learned over a specific training set.
The holdout method can be repeated several times to obtain a distribution of the test error rates, an approach known as random subsampling or the repeated holdout method.
This repeated approach produces a distribution of the error rates that can be used to understand the variance of the test error rate.
Random subsampling is a model evaluation technique that repeats random hold-out splits several times and averages the resulting performance scores.
Random subsampling does not guarantee that every instance is tested exactly once; some instances may be tested repeatedly while others may not be tested at all.
This approach is more stable than a single hold-out split, which suffers from high dependence on one specific division of the data.
Random subsampling is related to simple random sampling, where there is an equal probability of selecting any particular object.

Sampling can be conducted with or without replacement; in sampling with replacement, objects are not removed from the population as they are selected, allowing the same object to be picked more than once.
In sampling with replacement, the probability of selecting any object remains constant during the sampling process, particularly when samples are relatively small compared to the data set size.
k-Fold cross validation is a model evaluation technique that generalizes the holdout approach by segmenting the labeled data into k equal-sized partitions, or folds.
In each of the k runs, one partition is designated as the test set while the remaining k-1 partitions are used as the training set.
This process is repeated until every fold has served as the test set exactly once, ensuring that every data instance is used for both training and testing across the full procedure.
A different model is learned at every run, and the performance of each model on its respective test fold is aggregated to compute the overall test error rate.
The choice of k depends on the characteristics of the problem.
A small value of k results in smaller training sets for each run, which can lead to a larger estimate of generalization error rate than expected for a model trained on the entire labeled set.
A high value of k results in larger training sets, reducing the bias in the estimate of generalization error rate.
Choosing k between 5 and 10 provides a reasonable approach for estimating generalization error rate, as each fold can utilize 80% to 90% of the labeled data for training.
An extreme case occurs when k equals N, known as the leave-one-out approach, where every run uses exactly one data instance for testing and the remainder for training.
Standard k-fold cross validation produces a single estimate of the generalization error rate without providing information about the variance of that estimate.
To obtain variance information, one can run cross-validation for every possible partitioning of the data into k partitions, an approach known as complete cross-validation.

A more practical solution is to repeat the cross-validation approach multiple times using different random partitionings of the data into k partitions at each iteration, and use the average test error rate as the estimate.
Standard k-fold cross validation does not guarantee that the fraction of positive and negative instances in every partition is equal to the fraction observed in the overall data.
Stratified cross-validation performs stratified sampling of positive and negative instances into the k partitions to preserve class distribution.
Leave-one-out cross-validation (LOOCV) is a special case of k-fold cross-validation where the number of folds k equals the total number of data instances N.
In each run of LOOCV, exactly one data instance is held out for testing, and the model is trained on the remaining N − 1 instances.
This configuration provides the maximum possible training data per run, which reduces the bias in the estimate of the generalization error rate compared to using a smaller number of folds.
LOOCV is computationally expensive for large data sets because the model must be trained and evaluated N times.
Because there is only one possible partitioning of the data for the leave-one-out approach, it is not possible to estimate the variance of the generalization error rate.

LOOCV is distinct from standard k-fold cross-validation (where k is typically between 5 and 10), stratified cross-validation (which preserves class proportions), and bootstrap sampling (which samples with replacement and tests on out-of-bag instances).

Bootstrap sampling is a statistical resampling technique in which data instances are randomly selected with replacement from an original data set to create a synthetic collection of the same size as the original.
The sampling is done with replacement, allowing some instances to appear several times in the same training set, while others may be omitted.
On average, a bootstrap sample of size N contains approximately 63.2% of the unique instances from the original data, leaving about 36.8% of the instances unselected.
These unselected instances are known as out-of-bag instances and can be used as a test set for model evaluation.

The procedure is typically repeated multiple times to generate different training and test sets, allowing for the computation of distributions of performance measures such as accuracy, precision, and recall, or to estimate the distribution of the support of a frequent itemset.

In the context of ensemble methods like bagging (bootstrap aggregating), bootstrap sampling is used to train multiple classifiers on different subsets of the data, with the final prediction determined by majority voting.
The method is distinguished from k-fold cross-validation, which systematically splits data into subsets, and from hold-out methods, which split data once into training and test sets.

Stratified k-fold cross validation is a model evaluation technique that extends standard k-fold cross validation by ensuring that each fold approximately preserves the class distribution of the full dataset.

Stratified cross validation performs a stratified sampling of the positive and negative instances into the k partitions to keep the proportion of class labels in every fold the same as that of the overall data.
In standard k-fold cross validation, the labeled data is segmented into k equal-sized partitions, or folds.
During each run of standard k-fold cross validation, one partition is used for testing while the remaining partitions are used for training.
The process of standard k-fold cross validation is repeated until every fold has served as the test set once.

A key limitation of standard k-fold cross validation is that it does not guarantee that the fraction of positive and negative instances in every partition is equal to the fraction observed in the overall data.
Stratified k-fold cross validation is particularly useful for classification tasks where class imbalance might otherwise skew the evaluation results.
An empirical study by Kohavi suggests that ten-fold stratified cross validation is the best estimation method for performance metrics when compared to random subsampling and other k-fold variants.
Stratified k-fold cross validation is distinct from leave-one-out cross validation, which is a special case where k equals the total number of instances N.
Stratified k-fold cross validation is distinct from bootstrap sampling, which samples with replacement to form training sets and evaluates on out-of-bag instances.
Feature selection chooses a subset of the original features according to an evaluation criterion.

The purpose of feature selection is to remove irrelevant or redundant features, reduce dimensionality and acquisition or computational cost, and simplify the resulting model while retaining useful information.
Feature selection is a search over possible feature subsets, organized around a subset-evaluation measure, a search strategy, a stopping criterion, and validation.
Standard approaches to feature selection include embedded, filter, and wrapper methods.
Feature selection retains a subset of the original attributes rather than creating new combined attributes.
Feature selection differs from feature-construction methods in that it retains original attributes rather than creating new ones.
Redundant features are attributes that duplicate much or all of the information contained in one or more other attributes.
A common example of redundant features is the purchase price of a product and the amount of sales tax paid, which contain much of the same information.
The objective of feature selection is to identify important features and discard others as redundant or irrelevant.
Redundant features can reduce classification accuracy and the quality of clusters found, and in probability models like Naive Bayes, they can cause similar evidence to be counted twice.
Inter-feature redundancy is typically assessed by measuring association or correlation between pairs of selected features.
The choice of measure depends on the data type: Pearson correlation is used for numerical features, Spearman correlation for ordinal features, and the chi-square test for categorical features.
If two input features are strongly related or associated, one may be redundant.
Removal decisions should also consider cost, missingness, interpretability, and performance.
Consistency measures offer another approach by aiming to find a minimum number of features that separate classes as well as the full set, defined by the condition P(C|FullSet) = P(C|SubSet).
An inconsistency occurs when two examples have the same feature values but different class labels.
Using consistency measures allows for the removal of both irrelevant and redundant features.
Decision trees can also handle redundant attributes because redundant attributes show similar gains in purity, leading the algorithm to select only one of them as a split condition.
An attribute is defined as irrelevant if it is not useful for the classification task.
Irrelevant attributes are poorly associated with the target class labels, they provide little or no gain in purity and are typically passed over by other more relevant features.
The presence of a small number of irrelevant attributes will not impact the decision tree construction process.

If the classification problem is complex and there are a large number of irrelevant attributes, some of these attributes may be accidentally chosen during the tree-growing process because they may provide a better gain than a relevant attribute just by random chance.
Redundant and irrelevant features can reduce classification accuracy and the quality of the clusters that are found.
Feature selection techniques can help to improve the accuracy of decision trees by eliminating the irrelevant attributes during preprocessing.
In minimum subset techniques, an algorithm returns a minimum feature subset and no difference is made for features in the subset; whatever is relevant within the subset is otherwise irrelevant.
In search directions where the feature set shrinks and the subset grows, the subset may store only the irrelevant features.
Students' ID numbers are irrelevant to the task of predicting students' grade point averages.
The curse of dimensionality is the phenomenon that data analysis becomes increasingly difficult as the number of attributes grows.
The data space expands rapidly and observations become sparse, which can make distances and density differences less informative and local neighborhoods less meaningful.
These effects can degrade methods that depend on proximity or density, including clustering and classification methods.
This is a major motivation for dimensionality reduction and feature selection.

Kernel methods can avoid explicitly constructing coordinates in a transformed high-dimensional feature space, but that computational device does not eliminate the broader high-dimensional data problem.
The Filter Approach is one of three standard approaches to feature selection, alongside embedded and wrapper methods.
The Filter Approach operates independently of the data mining method subsequently employed.
Filter methods evaluate a subset of features independently of the downstream model.
The name 'filter' derives from the process of filtering undesirable features out before the learning phase begins.
Filter methods share components such as a measure for evaluating a subset, a search strategy, a stopping criterion, and a validation procedure.
Filter methods are usually faster than their wrapper counterparts because they are independent of the downstream model.
The Filter Approach is recommended for the detection and treatment of noisy data.
The Filter Approach is defined by its pre-learning feature evaluation and selection mechanism.
A ranker is a subcategory of filter feature-selection methods.
A ranker applies a criterion to score each feature independently and uses those scores to produce an ordering or ranking of the features.
The subsequent learning process, or a user-defined threshold, determines how many of the highest-ranked features are retained.
Ranking is performed independently of the particular learning algorithm that will later use the selected features.
The wrapper approach is a feature selection strategy that uses a learning algorithm as a black box to evaluate feature subsets, aiming to improve the predictive performance of that specific learner.
Wrapper methods are designed to select features that accomplish the highest predictive accuracy for a fixed learning algorithm.
The wrapper approach involves two stages: feature subset selection and re-learning the data mining model with the best subset.
Unlike filter methods, which cannot allow a learning algorithm to fully exploit its bias, wrapper methods can.
To avoid overfitting, the wrapper approach employs statistical validation, such as cross-validation, to agree on a predictive measure.
Wrapper approaches are an interesting choice in some domains.
Wrapper approaches require higher computational costs and are usually slower than filter methods.
Experimental studies have shown that results vary among learners, often recommending wrapper approaches for each kind of learner to optimize performance.

The filter versus wrapper trade-off in feature selection concerns the choice between two distinct evaluation strategies: filters evaluate features before learning, whereas wrappers evaluate subsets by using the learner.
Both filter and wrapper methods can be encompassed within a common architecture that includes a measure for evaluating a subset, a search strategy, a stopping criterion, and a validation procedure.
Filter methods and wrapper methods differ only in the way in which they evaluate a subset of features.
A wrapper model consists of two stages: feature subset selection and a stage that is the same as in the filter model.
Wrapper models can achieve the purpose of improving the particular learner's predictive performance.
The trade-off is that filter models cannot allow a learning algorithm to fully exploit its bias, whereas wrapper methods do.
Wrapper methods are usually slower than filters.
Filters are thought to be more appropriate than wrapper-based feature selectors under time constraints.
Sequential Forward Generation (SFG) is a forward feature-subset search direction.
SFG starts with an empty selected set S and adds one feature at a time according to the feature-subset criterion.
A stopping rule may specify the desired number of selected features or another criterion.
The stopping condition is met or all features have been considered when the algorithm stops adding features.
Whether the overall search strategy is exhaustive, heuristic, or nondeterministic is a separate design choice.
Sequential Backward Generation (SBG) is a heuristic feature selection method that starts with the full set of features and iteratively removes features one at a time.
The algorithm is defined by the function SBG(F, U), where F is the full set of features and U is the measure or criterion used to evaluate subsets.
The procedure initializes a set S to hold the removed features.
In a repeat loop, the algorithm selects the next feature to remove using f = GetNext(F) (or f = FindNextWorst(F, U) in the heuristic variant).
The algorithm removes the selected feature from the current set via F = F \setminus \{f\} and adds it to the removed set via S = S \cup \{f\}.
The loop continues until the remaining set F fails to satisfy the criterion U or until F becomes empty.
When the stopping condition is met, the algorithm returns F \cup \{f\}, where f is the last removed feature.
This return value is justified because f was the last feature removed, and after removing it, the remaining set failed the criterion.

SBG is distinguished from Sequential Forward Generation (SFG), which starts from an empty set and adds features, and from Bidirectional Generation (BG), which combines forward and backward search directions.
SBG is a heuristic method because it uses greedy choices to select the next worst feature to remove.

Bidirectional Generation (BG) is a feature set generation algorithm that begins the search in both directions, performing Sequential Forward Generation (SFG) and Sequential Backward Generation (SBG) concurrently.

The search terminates under one of two conditions: (1) when one search finds the best subset comprised of m features before it reaches the exact middle, or (2) when both searches achieve the middle of the search space.
The bidirectional generation is shown in operation in the algorithm.
Random Generation (RG) is a feature set generation algorithm that produces subsets of features at random.
The choice of adding or removing a feature is a random decision in Random Generation (RG).
Random Generation (RG) generates random subsets and returns the best satisfactory subset found when the stopping criterion is reached.
Random Generation (RG) is non-deterministic because the generated subsets are random.
Random Generation (RG) starts the search in a random direction.
Unlike Sequential Forward Generation (SFG) or Sequential Backward Generation (SBG), the size of the subset of features cannot be stipulated in Random Generation (RG).
A random generation scheme is based on a good random number generator attached with a function called RandGen(F).
The formal relation for Random Generation (RG) is S = RandGen(F).
Random Generation (RG) tries to avoid stagnation into a local optima by not following a fixed way for subset generation.
Exhaustive search is a feature selection strategy that explores the entire search space to identify the optimal subset of features.
Exhaustive search is defined by its completeness: it covers all possible combinations of features.
The method can be implemented in two primary directions: forward search and backward search.
In backward search, the process starts with the full set of features and iteratively removes features to find the optimal subset.
The space complexity of exhaustive search is O(2^M), where M is the total number of features.
If a threshold m is established for the minimum number of features to be selected, the search space is defined by the sum of combinations from 0 to m.
Exhaustive search is the only method that guarantees the optimality of the selected feature subset.
Exhaustive search is often impractical for large datasets due to its high computational cost.
Exact algorithms like backtracking and branch and bound can be used to find an optimal subset without visiting all possible states.
Exhaustive search is typically paired with evaluation measures such as probability, consistency, or accuracy.
Exhaustive search is considered a complete search strategy in the taxonomy of feature selection methods.
Heuristic search is a feature selection strategy that employs heuristics to carry out the search, preventing brute force exploration while ensuring the discovery of a non-optimal subset of features.
Heuristic search is positioned as a middle ground between exhaustive search and nondeterministic search.
The search process draws a path connecting the beginning and the end in a manner similar to depth-first search, where the maximum length of this path is M and the number of subsets generated is O(M).
The choice of the heuristic is crucial to finding a subset closer to the optimal one in a faster operation.
Heuristic search can be combined with different search directions, such as forward or backward, and evaluation measures.
Heuristic search is one of the three values for the Search Strategy dimension, alongside Complete and Nondeterministic.

One specific implementation of heuristic search is the Mutual Information based Feature Selection (MIFS), which uses a greedy algorithm to replace impossible exhaustive search by choosing the next feature that maximizes information about the class relative to the average mutual information with already selected features.
Non-Deterministic Search is a feature selection strategy also known as random search.
Non-Deterministic Search is characterized by the random choice of search direction.
The generated subsets in Non-Deterministic Search are random, allowing the method to avoid stagnation in local optima.
Non-Deterministic Search can generate best subsets constantly and keep improving the quality of selected features as time goes by.
It is unnecessary to wait until the search ends to obtain results in Non-Deterministic Search.
The algorithm knows which subset is better than the previous one and which one is the best at the moment in Non-Deterministic Search.
Non-Deterministic Search is one of the values for the Search strategy dimension, alongside Complete and Heuristic search.
Non-Deterministic Search is typically paired with a Random search direction.
The chi-squared test compares observed and expected counts in the contingency table of two categorical attributes A and B.
The null hypothesis of the chi-squared test is that the two categorical attributes are independent.
The chi-squared test uses (r-1)(c-1) degrees of freedom.
The chi-squared statistic is calculated as χ² = ∑_{i=1}^c ∑_{j=1}^r (o_ij-e_ij)²/e_ij, where e_ij = count(A=a_i)·count(B=b_j)/m.
A sufficiently large χ² value relative to the chosen significance level leads to rejection of independence and supports statistical association between the attributes.
The Pearson product-moment correlation coefficient is a dependence measure used to quantify the degree of linear correlation between two numerical variables.
The coefficient is calculated using the values of the two attributes, their respective means, and their standard deviations.
For two variables A and B, the correlation coefficient r_{A,B} is given by the formula: r_{A,B} = (Σ_{i=1}^{m} (a_i - A̅)(b_i - B̅)) / (m σ_A σ_B).
The Pearson product-moment correlation coefficient is described as the most well-known correlation coefficient.
It is specifically applied to numerical features to assess linear relationships.
An alternative formulation for variables X and Y is ρ(X,Y) = Σ_i (x_i - x̄)(y_i - ȳ) / [ (Σ_i (x_i - x̄)^2) (Σ_i (y_i - ȳ)^2) ]^{1/2}.
This measure is distinct from rank-based or categorical measures, as it specifically targets linear association in numeric data.

In the formula, m represents the number of instances, a_i and b_i are the values of attributes A and B in the instances, A̅ and B̅ are the mean values of A and B respectively, and σ_A and σ_B are the standard deviations of A and B.
Covariance is a statistical measure used to determine how much two variables change together.
The covariance between attributes A and B is given by the formula: Cov(A, B) = E((A - A̅)(B - B̅)) = (1/m) * Σᵢ₌₁ᵐ (aᵢ - A̅)(bᵢ - B̅).
The sign of the covariance indicates the direction of the relationship between the variables.
If two attributes vary similarly, such that when A is greater than its mean A̅, B is also likely to be greater than its mean B̅, the covariance is positive.
If one attribute tends to be above its expected value while the other is below its expected value, the covariance is negative.
When the two variables are independent, the expected value of their product equals the product of their expected values (E(A·B) = E(A)·E(B)), which results in a covariance of zero.
A covariance of zero does not necessarily imply that the attributes are independent, as some random variables may have a covariance of zero while still being dependent.
Covariance is closely related to the Pearson product-moment correlation coefficient.
The correlation coefficient r(A,B) is calculated by dividing the covariance of A and B by the product of their standard deviations: r(A,B) = Cov(A, B) / (σA * σB).
Covariance can be used in assessing redundancy between numerical attributes, as high correlation (derived from covariance) may indicate that one attribute can be removed.
Spearman Rank Correlation is a measure of association defined as the Pearson correlation computed on the ranks of the variables.
The Spearman correlation coefficient is formally expressed as r_s = ρ(R(X), R(Y)).
Spearman correlation is specifically used for ordinal variables, ranked variables, or numerical variables where a monotonic relationship is more important than a linear relationship.

In contrast to Pearson correlation, which measures linear relationships between numerical variables, Spearman correlation measures monotonic relationships by applying the Pearson calculation to ranks.
The resulting value of Spearman correlation falls within the range [−1, 1].
A value of 0 indicates no monotonic relationship in Spearman correlation.
When calculating Spearman correlation in the presence of tied values, the procedure requires using average ranks and computing the Pearson correlation on those ranks.
Information Gain (Feature Goodness) is a criterion used in feature selection to evaluate how well a feature reduces uncertainty in a dataset.
The information gain from a feature A, denoted as IG(A), is defined as the difference between the prior uncertainty and the expected posterior uncertainty using A.
The information gain is expressed as IG(A) = I(D) - ∑_{j=1}^{p} (|D_j| / |D|) I(D_j^A).

In the context of predictive learning, the 'message' is the output feature or class in classification, and an information measure U is defined such that larger values represent higher levels of uncertainty.
A feature evaluation model inferred from this concept states that feature Ai is chosen instead of feature Aj if IG(Ai) > IG(Aj), meaning Ai reduces more uncertainty than Aj.
This idea is used in algorithms like C4.5 for selecting a feature to generate new branches.

Information Gain is biased toward attributes with many distinct values; for example, if an attribute has a unique value for each instance (such as an ID), a multiway split can create one pure child node per instance, resulting in zero weighted child entropy and maximal Information Gain.
Shannon entropy is a measure for quantifying uncertainty in classification contexts.
The mathematical formulation for entropy is given by the formula: Entropy = −∑(i=0 to c−1) p_i(t) log_2 p_i(t), where p_i(t) represents the probability of class i at time t.
Shannon entropy is frequently employed to define information gain, which motivates the concept as a measure of uncertainty reduction.
In specific applications, such as a binary classification problem with equal class distributions, the entropy value can reach 1, indicating maximal uncertainty.
For instance, a calculation for a parent node with 10 positive and 10 negative instances yields an entropy of 1, demonstrating the measure's behavior in balanced datasets.

Shannon entropy is distinct from information gain, which uses entropy to evaluate the reduction in uncertainty after a split, and from gain ratio, which adjusts for the number of distinct values in an attribute to mitigate bias toward high-cardinality features.
The null hypothesis (H0) is a formal statement in statistical testing that serves as the baseline assumption to be evaluated against observed data.
The null hypothesis represents the distribution of a test statistic under the assumption that no effect or difference exists.
The primary role of the null hypothesis is to enable the calculation of a p-value, which is the probability of falsely rejecting H0 when it is actually true.
The null hypothesis is explicitly defined alongside an alternative hypothesis (H1) to provide a rigorous framework for assessing whether an observed result is statistically significant.
In anomaly detection, H0 states that an instance belongs to the normal class.
In classifier evaluation, the null hypothesis states that the classifier has not learned a generalizable relationship between attributes and class labels.
Failing to reject the null hypothesis is not equivalent to accepting it.
A non-significant result may still arise from the alternative distribution or a misspecified null model.
The null hypothesis provides the reference distribution against which the extremity of a test statistic is measured to determine if it falls within a critical region.
A test statistic is a numerical quantity used to quantify the evidence in an observed outcome with respect to a null hypothesis.
The test statistic measures how extreme an observed result is under the null hypothesis.
The definition of extreme depends on the choice of the null hypothesis and the design of the test statistic.
The test statistic typically summarizes every possible outcome as a single count or real-valued value, enabling the computation of the probability of an outcome under the null hypothesis.
An observed test statistic can be considered extreme if it is greater than or equal to a certain value, smaller than or equal to a certain value, or outside a specified interval.
The test statistic is chosen to differentiate the behavior of results under the null hypothesis from the behavior of results under the alternative hypothesis.
The distribution of the test statistic under the null hypothesis must be modeled to conduct hypothesis testing.
The p-value of an observed test statistic is the probability of obtaining that value or something more extreme from the null distribution.
The test statistic is used in various contexts, including cluster analysis, anomaly detection, and association analysis.
In cluster analysis, the test statistic is typically a cluster validity measure used to test whether the observed clustering is significant compared to random partitioning.
In anomaly detection, the anomaly score of an instance serves as the test statistic, with the null hypothesis that the instance belongs to the normal class.
In association analysis, the test statistic measures the deviation of an observed contingency table from the null hypothesis of no association among items.
A primary requirement for conducting statistical testing is knowing how the test statistic is distributed under the null hypothesis.
The distribution of the test statistic can be estimated by fitting statistical models or by using non-parametric approaches.
Increasing the sample size helps obtain less variable estimates of the true null and alternative distributions.
The significance level, denoted by α, is a fixed threshold on p-values that is decided before any tests are performed.
A result is called statistically significant if its p-value is lower than the significance level threshold.
The p-value of a statistically significant result denotes the probability of falsely rejecting the null hypothesis when it is true.
Common choices for the significance level include 0.05 (5%) and 0.01 (1%).

Rejecting the null hypothesis if the test statistic falls in the critical region is equivalent to evaluating the p-value and rejecting the null hypothesis if the p-value falls below the pre-specified threshold.
In the context of multiple hypothesis testing, the significance level can be adjusted to balance power and false positives.
The Benjamini-Hochberg (BH) procedure adjusts the significance level for the i-th p-value as αi = i × α/m.

The BH procedure declares the first k p-values as significant, where k is the largest index such that the p-value is lower than its significance level, guaranteeing that the False Discovery Rate (FDR) is smaller than α.
One-sided and two-sided tests are distinct approaches to statistical hypothesis testing that differ in how the probability of the null distribution is allocated across its tails.
A one-sided test concentrates the entire probability of the significance level into a single tail of the distribution.
A two-sided test splits the probability of the significance level equally between both tails of the distribution.
The choice between one-sided and two-sided tests depends on the specific research question.
A one-sided test is used when the hypothesis is directional, such as testing whether one entity is better than another.
A two-sided test is used when the hypothesis is non-directional, asking whether two entities are different in either direction.

A low p-value in either type of test indicates smaller probabilities in the tails of the null distribution, providing sufficient evidence to believe that the observed result is a significant departure from the null hypothesis and justifying its rejection.
In the context of classifier comparison, a two-tailed test typically uses a threshold such as |Z| > 1.96 at a significance level of 0.05 to determine if classifiers are significantly different.
